analysis.one_liner: Blocks a federal rule setting minimum nurse staffing levels and pay transparency in nursing homes.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 26 cosponsors on February 13, 2025, the bill has sat in two House committees without a hearing or vote; the 2024 staffing rule it targets has not been repealed.
analysis.plain_summary: In May 2024, the federal agency that runs Medicare and Medicaid issued a rule requiring nursing homes that receive Medicare and Medicaid money to provide a minimum amount of nursing care — a nurse on site around the clock and at least 3.48 hours of nursing care per resident per day — and requiring states to report how Medicaid payments actually reach the workers who provide direct care. This bill would forbid the government from putting any of that rule into effect, and would also bar any "substantially similar" future regulation. It has not moved since it was referred to two House committees in February 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home operators, who would avoid the cost of hiring additional nurses and aides to meet the staffing minimums and would avoid public reporting of how Medicaid dollars reach direct-care staff.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from implementing, administering, or enforcing the CMS rule published May 10, 2024, titled "Minimum Staffing Standards for Long-Term Care Facilities and Medicaid Institutional Payment Transparency Reporting."
The rule it blocks would require an onsite registered nurse 24 hours a day and a minimum of 3.48 total nurse staffing hours per resident per day in Medicare and Medicaid long-term care facilities.
It would also block a requirement that state Medicaid programs report on payments to direct care workers and support staff of nursing facilities and intermediate care facilities.
The prohibition extends to "any substantially similar regulation," which would prevent a future administration from issuing a comparable staffing standard.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home residents and their families, who would not get the staffing levels the rule was designed to guarantee, and direct care workers, whose pay transparency requirement would be scrapped. Residents of understaffed facilities face higher risks of falls, pressure injuries, and neglect when too few caregivers cover too many residents.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home residents and direct care workers

drawbacks.text: Blocking the rule means nursing homes face no federal minimum on how much nursing care each resident receives each day, leaving staffing levels to facilities that already operate with thin rosters.

It cancels the requirement that states disclose how Medicaid payments actually reach the aides and nurses who deliver care, removing a check on whether public long-term-care dollars pay for care or for facility overhead.
Because the bill bars "any substantially similar regulation," it would tie the hands of future administrations from setting any comparable staffing standard, not just the 2024 rule.

The honest cost an operator would point to: meeting the staffing minimums requires hiring nurses and aides in a labor market where such workers are scarce, and facilities argued they could not absorb that cost without cutting capacity. That objection does not answer the transparency provisions, which impose no staffing mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit flows to a specific industry — lower labor costs and no disclosure of how Medicaid money is spent — while the cost falls on the residents of nursing homes, a population that is among the least able to advocate for itself. The staffing standards had phase-in timelines built into the rule precisely to spread hiring costs over years; this bill removes the standards outright rather than adjusting them. On balance, the costs to residents outweigh the savings to operators.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to two House committees in February 2025, and neither committee has held a hearing or brought it to a vote, so it sits untouched while the Congress continues.

narrative.text: Rep. Michelle Fischbach (R-MN) introduced the bill on February 13, 2025, with 18 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction.
26 members cosponsored the bill — 25 of 223 House Republicans and 1 of 216 House Democrats.
The full action history shows no action after the referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action as of the latest update.
The 2024 CMS rule the bill targets, including the 3.48 nursing hours per resident per day standard, has not been repealed by Congress in this session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home residents and direct care workers are better off for now, because the bill that would nullify the staffing minimums and pay transparency reporting has not advanced. Nursing home operators retain their existing staffing obligations under the 2024 rule rather than gaining the relief this bill offered.

for.name: Michelle Fischbach
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to block the 2024 CMS nursing home staffing rule and recruited original cosponsors.

for.name: American Health Care Association
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against the 2024 federal staffing mandate and urged Congress to overturn it.

sides.party_line_note: Support is nearly all Republican: 25 of the 26 cosponsors are House Republicans, with a single House Democrat, and no member has acted against it because the bill has never reached a hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Nursing home and long-term care operators
industries.note: The bill saves operators the cost of meeting the 3.48 nurse hours per resident per day minimum and the 24/7 onsite nurse requirement, and spares them disclosure of how Medicaid payments reach care staff. Those savings come directly at the expense of guaranteed care levels for residents.

industries.industry: Direct care workers (nurses' aides and facility nursing staff)
industries.note: The bill eliminates the requirement that Medicaid programs report what direct care workers are actually paid, removing pressure for wages to flow to staff. The staffing mandate itself would have meant more hiring demand for these workers; blocking it removes both the transparency and the jobs the mandate would create.

analysis.trajectory: Bills to overturn a regulation rarely move on their own without a committee hearing and leadership backing; with no action eight months after referral to two committees, the likely path is that this bill stalls in committee for the rest of the 119th Congress. Provisions blocking the staffing rule are more likely to reappear as riders on a large funding bill, which does not require a standalone vote, than to reach the floor as H.R. 1303.
